S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.

subtypes.Contamination Obsessions: Recurrent and intrusive worries about contamination, germs, or dirt.
subtypes.Pathological Doubt: Pathological doubt regarding safety or mistakes, such as whether doors are locked or gas valves are closed.
subtypes.Symmetry and Exactness Obsessions: A strong urge that items must be lined up exactly or be symmetrical.
subtypes.Forbidden or Taboo Thoughts: Intrusive thoughts involving aggressive (harming others), sexual, or religious content that are prohibited.
subtypes.Somatic Obsessions: Persistent and specific fear that one might have a serious disease.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.

subtypes.Cleaning or Washing Compulsions: Repetitive acts to remove contamination, such as hand washing, showering, or excessive cleaning.
subtypes.Checking Compulsions: Repeatedly checking items like door locks, gas stoves, or switches to prevent danger.
subtypes.Ordering and Arranging Compulsions: Organizing objects in a specific order or at a precise angle to reduce anxiety.
subtypes.Mental Acts: Mental rituals performed internally, such as praying, counting, or repeating specific words silently.
subtypes.Repeating Rituals: Repeating specific actions (e.g., standing up, passing through a door) a set number of times.

symptom.disease_info: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is characterized by recurrent, intrusive thoughts, images, or urges (obsessions) and/or repetitive behaviors or mental acts (compulsions) that the person feels driven to perform. These experiences are time-consuming or cause significant distress and impairment, and the individual typically recognizes that the thoughts or behaviors are excessive or unreasonable. Onset is often in adolescence or early adulthood, with a chronic but fluctuating course that may worsen during periods of stress or role change. OCD is distinguished from anxiety disorders and psychotic disorders by the presence of ego-dystonic, ritual-driven phenomena that are not better explained by delusions, generalized worry, or a primary mood disturbance.

patient.stressor: Jose had been slowly working his way from hands-on construction jobs toward a supervisory role in construction management, taking evening certification courses while helping coordinate community renovation projects. Over the past few years, as he took on more responsibility for safety checks, budgets, and permits, he began spending more and more time redoing the same planning tasks and second-guessing every small decision, which led to missed deadlines and frustration from supervisors. When a series of delays and conflicts over his reliability caused him to lose a foreman opportunity and eventually step out of the workforce, he tried to compensate by taking on elaborate DIY projects and volunteering more at the community center, only to find the same patterns interfering with basic tasks at home, like getting meals on the table or leaving the house on time. His wife and extended family finally urged him to see a psychiatrist after he abandoned another construction-management course because he felt "paralyzed" by certain thoughts during exams and planning assignments, leaving him despondent about his ability to support the family.
patient.chief_complaint: “I get stuck doing the same checks and routines over and over until I can’t finish anything, even when I know it makes no sense.”

patient.stressor: As Sophia moved into a senior designer role and began informally preparing for a creative director position, her workload shifted from mostly hands-on design to more client-facing presentations, high-stakes brand launches, and mentoring junior staff. Around this transition, she noticed that projects she once handled fluidly now stalled because she spent hours mentally reviewing the same design decisions and repeatedly revisiting minor details, which pushed her into frequent deadline crunches and late nights at the studio. Her usual coping outlets—yoga, gardening, and travel—started to feel crowded out by the time she spent stuck at her desk and ruminating at home, leading to tension with her spouse when last-minute work overrides derailed planned trips and weekends. After a particularly public stumble during a client pitch, where she froze because she couldn’t get past certain distressing thoughts about the presentation being "wrong," her manager gently suggested she talk to a professional about how much her inner doubts were interfering with her work, prompting her to seek psychiatric evaluation.
patient.chief_complaint: “I can’t shut off these repeating thoughts about my work being wrong, and they take over until I’m missing deadlines.”

patient.stressor: In his early fifties, Edgar managed a demanding systems architect role while staying active in Northern Cheyenne community events and mentoring Indigenous youth in coding. When his older sister in South Dakota developed serious cardiac and mobility problems, he began traveling frequently to help coordinate her care and manage medical paperwork, all while trying to maintain his leadership role at work. The responsibility of overseeing complex technical systems by day and navigating medical decisions and travel logistics by night seemed to trigger a longstanding tendency to overanalyze and double-check into something more consuming, leaving him increasingly preoccupied and unable to relax even during hikes or drumming sessions. After he missed a critical configuration change at work because he had spent so long mentally going over unrelated worries that he delayed the task until the last minute, and then found himself lying awake for hours caught in the same mental loops, a colleague and close friend from the hikers club urged him to seek psychiatric help, noting that he seemed "trapped in his head" even on the trail.
patient.chief_complaint: “My mind keeps getting stuck on the same upsetting thoughts about messing things up for my family and at work, and I can’t let them go.”
